title: Prayer, Work, and the Lord’s Peace
summary: Paul requests prayer, trusts the faithful Lord, commands disciplined work and restorative correction of the disorderly, and closes with peace, grace, and his own signature.
historicalContext: Paul wrote this letter from Corinth not long after the first, while he, Silvanus, and Timothy faced organized resistance from members of the synagogue that eventually brought him before the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:5–17). In Thessalonica a young church of mostly Gentile converts was enduring hostility from fellow citizens and had been unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord had already arrived. Some members had stopped working and were living on the generosity of others while busying themselves in other people’s affairs. Paul had addressed the matter during his founding visit and again in his first letter (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; 5:14), yet the problem had grown. In a city where manual labor was widely looked down upon and wealthy patrons often kept dependents, the conduct of believers was plainly visible to neighbors who would judge the gospel by what they saw.
literaryContext: Chapter 3 holds the letter’s final exhortations and its closing. Verses 1–5 form a transitional unit: a request for prayer, an assurance of the Lord’s faithfulness, an expression of confidence, and a short wish-prayer, each preparing the readers to receive the commands that follow. Verses 6–15 then take up the disorderly, framed by matching instructions to withdraw (v. 6) and to keep no company with the disobedient (v. 14), and supported by Paul’s example (vv. 7–9) and his earlier teaching (v. 10). The closing (vv. 16–18) gathers the whole letter together. The Lord of peace answers the fears of chapters 1 and 2 and the tensions of chapter 3, Paul’s handwritten greeting answers the danger of letters falsely bearing his name (2:2), and the repeated “all” embraces even those under correction.
themes: Intercession for the advance of the gospel
The faithfulness of Christ amid human unbelief
Hope that endures and keeps working
Example and teaching in Christian formation
Peace and grace for the whole church

outline.title: Prayer and Confidence in the Faithful Lord
outline.summary: Paul asks prayer for the gospel’s progress and his deliverance, then assures the church of Christ’s guarding faithfulness and prays for their hearts.

outline.title: The Command, the Example, and the Rule
outline.summary: The church is to withdraw from members who live disorderly, remembering the apostles’ self-supporting labor and the rule that the unwilling should not eat.

outline.title: Correcting the Disorderly as Brothers
outline.summary: Idle meddlers are told to work steadily, the faithful are urged not to tire of doing good, and discipline is to be firm yet brotherly.

outline.title: Peace, Signature, and Grace
outline.summary: Paul prays for the Lord’s peace and presence, authenticates the letter in his own hand, and commends all to Christ’s grace.

verses.bibleText: Finally, brethren, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may have free course, and be glorified, even as it is with you:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Finally” in Paul seldom signals that a letter is about to stop. Here it turns the reader from the long argument about the day of the Lord to the practical matters that remain: prayer, confidence, the problem of those who refuse to work, and the closing blessing. The word marks a transition more than an ending, and the requests that follow grow out of what has just been said. Paul has prayed that Christ and the Father would comfort and establish the Thessalonians (2:16–17); now he asks them to carry him and his companions to God in return.

The request is striking for its order. Writing from Corinth, where opposition was gathering (Acts 18:5–6), Paul asks first for the progress of the message and only afterward for his own safety. He wants “the word of the Lord” to “have free course,” literally to run. Scripture had already pictured God’s word racing across the earth to do His bidding (Psalm 147:15), and Paul’s readers knew the footraces of the Greek games. The gospel is imagined as a runner moving swiftly along an open course and then receiving the honor due a victor. That honor comes when hearers accept the message for what it is, the word of God, and when changed lives display its power (1 Thessalonians 2:13; Titus 2:10).

“Even as it is with you” is a brief but warm commendation. The Thessalonians themselves were evidence that the word could run. It had come to them “in power, and in the Holy Ghost” and had sounded out from their city through Macedonia and Achaia (1 Thessalonians 1:5–8). Paul asks them to pray that what happened among them would happen in Corinth and beyond.

The verse also reveals how the apostle viewed his own labor. He did not suppose that eloquence or persistence would carry the gospel forward. The Lord who opened hearts in Macedonia must open doors elsewhere (Colossians 4:3), and He has chosen to work in answer to the prayers of His people. Intercession is therefore real participation in mission. A church that cannot travel with the missionary can still labor beside him before the throne of grace.

wordNotes.term: τρέχῃ καὶ δοξάζηται (trechē kai doxazētai) — may have free course, and be glorified
wordNotes.explanation: The first verb means “run,” and the present tense pictures the message continuing on its way. Joined with “be glorified,” it suggests a runner who completes the course and is publicly honored. The word is glorified when people receive it as God’s message and when obedient lives commend it to others.

wordNotes.term: τὸ λοιπόν (to loipon) — finally
wordNotes.explanation: Paul uses this expression to move to the remaining business of a letter, often well before the end. It introduces what follows from the preceding discussion rather than announcing an immediate close.

verses.bibleText: And that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men: for all men have not faith.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second request follows from the first. If the word is to run, its messengers must not be silenced, so Paul asks prayer “that we may be delivered from unreasonable and wicked men.” The verb speaks of rescue from danger, and the definite article in Greek (“the unreasonable and wicked men”) suggests that he had particular opponents in view. Acts records that at Corinth members of the synagogue resisted and reviled him and later dragged him before the proconsul Gallio (Acts 18:6, 12–13). In the same period the Lord assured Paul in a night vision that no one would harm him there, and he remained a year and a half (Acts 18:9–11). The Thessalonians’ prayers may well have been part of that deliverance.

“Unreasonable” renders a word meaning “out of place.” It describes conduct that is morally absurd, behavior with no fitting place in God’s ordered world. Paired with “wicked,” it portrays opponents whose hostility is both irrational and malicious. Paul does not name them or describe their schemes; the Thessalonians, who had watched a similar mob gather in their own streets (Acts 17:5–9), needed no explanation.

“For all men have not faith” is an understatement with weight behind it. Many who heard the gospel refused it, and some hardened themselves until they turned against those who preached it. Faith here is the trusting response to the message, and Scripture never treats it as automatic. The same word that softens one heart may harden another that resists the Spirit’s pleading (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). Paul’s remark guards believers against surprise: rejection does not mean the gospel has failed. It also prepares a wordplay, for the faithlessness of people in this verse is about to be set beside the faithfulness of the Lord in the next.

wordNotes.term: ἀτόπων καὶ πονηρῶν (atopōn kai ponērōn) — unreasonable and wicked
wordNotes.explanation: Atopos literally means “out of place” and, used of conduct, describes what is improper or perverse. Ponēros is the common word for what is evil or malicious. Together they portray opponents whose actions are both senseless and harmful.

wordNotes.term: οὐ γὰρ πάντων ἡ πίστις (ou gar pantōn hē pistis) — for all men have not faith
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase is a deliberate understatement meaning that many do not believe. Faith here is the human response of trust to the word of the Lord. Its absence explains both the need for the gospel to run and the danger its preachers face.

verses.bibleText: But the Lord is faithful, who shall stablish you, and keep you from evil.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But the Lord is faithful.” In Greek the last word of verse 2 is “faith” and the first word of verse 3 is “faithful,” two nearly identical terms placed side by side. The contrast is intended. Many people have no faith; the Lord never lacks faithfulness. What Paul cannot count on from human beings he can count on from Christ, and the assurance is so firm that he turns at once from his own danger to the needs of his readers.

The faithful one is “the Lord,” who throughout this letter is Jesus Christ (2:16; 3:5, 16). Elsewhere Paul writes “God is faithful” (1 Corinthians 1:9; 10:13); here he applies the same covenant attribute to the Son with no sense of strain. The faithfulness Moses celebrated in the God who keeps covenant (Deuteronomy 7:9) belongs equally to the risen Lord who keeps His people.

Two actions follow. He “shall stablish you,” the verb Paul used in his prayer at 2:17, now stated as a confident promise. He will “keep you from evil,” guarding the believers as a sentry guards a city. The Greek may be read either as evil in general or as “the evil one.” The personal sense suits the setting. This letter has just described Satan’s working behind the lawless power “with all power and signs and lying wonders” (2:9), and Jesus taught His disciples to pray for deliverance from the evil one (Matthew 6:13). The struggle the Thessalonians faced belonged to the larger controversy between Christ and Satan, and the outcome of that controversy is settled.

The promise does not exempt believers from hardship. Paul had warned them from the beginning that affliction would come (1 Thessalonians 3:3–4). What the Lord guarantees is that no power of evil can tear from His hand those who continue to trust Him. Strength for each day and protection against the adversary are gifts of His faithfulness, received by faith.

wordNotes.term: πιστὸς δέ ἐστιν ὁ κύριος (pistos de estin ho kyrios) — but the Lord is faithful
wordNotes.explanation: Paul elsewhere says that God is faithful; here the title “Lord” points to Christ. The adjective pistos stands immediately after the noun pistis that closes verse 2, sharpening the contrast between human unbelief and the Lord’s unfailing reliability.

wordNotes.term: φυλάξει ἀπὸ τοῦ πονηροῦ (phylaxei apo tou ponērou) — keep you from evil
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to guard or protect, as a watchman protects what is entrusted to him. The phrase can be translated “from evil” or “from the evil one.” The surrounding references to Satan’s activity make the personal sense likely, though the protection extends to every evil he employs.

verses.bibleText: And we have confidence in the Lord touching you, that ye both do and will do the things which we command you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul’s next sentence rests on the one before. Because the Lord is faithful, the apostle can say, “we have confidence in the Lord touching you.” The ground of his assurance lies in Christ, who is at work in them, more than in the Thessalonians’ own resolve. This is how Paul speaks of other churches when he trusts that the One who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6; Galatians 5:10).

The content of that confidence is obedience: “ye both do and will do the things which we command you.” The commands are not yet stated, but the verb “command” looks ahead to verses 6, 10, and 12, where the instructions about work and discipline are given. Paul commends the church before he corrects some of its members. Most of the congregation was already living as he had taught, and his expressed confidence encourages them to continue while making the disobedient few more conspicuous.

The verse holds together two truths that are sometimes pulled apart. Obedience is something believers actually do, and Paul expects it of them. Yet it happens “in the Lord,” enabled by His grace and sustained by His faithfulness. The commands of Christ come with the power of the One who gives them, so that those who receive them in faith are able to keep them.

wordNotes.term: πεποίθαμεν … ἐν κυρίῳ (pepoithamen … en kyriō) — we have confidence in the Lord
wordNotes.explanation: The perfect tense describes a settled conviction. Its anchor is “in the Lord,” meaning that Paul’s optimism about the church rests on Christ’s presence and work among them.

wordNotes.term: παραγγέλλομεν (parangellomen) — we command
wordNotes.explanation: This verb carries the tone of an authoritative instruction, firmer than Paul’s usual “we beseech.” Its use here prepares for the repeated commands about work and discipline in verses 6–12.

verses.bibleText: And the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God, and into the patient waiting for Christ.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Confidence turns again into prayer. “The Lord direct your hearts” uses a verb meaning to make straight, the same one Paul used when he prayed that God would clear his road back to Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3:11). Here the road is inward. The heart, which in Scripture includes thought, desire, and will, easily wanders after many things, and Paul asks Christ to set it on a straight course toward two destinations. The Old Testament often speaks of preparing or directing the heart toward God (1 Chronicles 29:18; 2 Chronicles 19:3), and the apostle now addresses that request to the Lord Jesus.

The first destination is “the love of God.” The phrase can mean love for God, but Paul’s usage elsewhere points chiefly to God’s own love for His people (Romans 5:5; 8:39), and only a few verses earlier he described the Father as the One “which hath loved us” (2:16). A heart steadily directed into that love will answer with love in return and will find strength to obey the instructions that follow.

The second destination is “the patient waiting for Christ.” The Greek noun ordinarily means steadfast endurance, and the phrase reads literally “the endurance of Christ.” It may point to the steadfastness Christ Himself showed in His sufferings, which believers are called to share, or to the patient endurance that marks those who wait for Him. The familiar rendering captures a real thread in this letter. Some at Thessalonica had been unsettled by claims that the day of Christ had already come (2:2), and some had abandoned daily labor. The remedy was a settled, enduring hope that keeps working, loving, and standing firm until the Lord appears, free from both feverish excitement and indifference.

These two destinations belong together. God’s love gives the heart its security; Christlike endurance gives it staying power. A church grounded in both can wait for the Second Coming without drifting into speculation or idleness and can meet pressure without losing its footing (Hebrews 12:2–3; James 5:7–8).

wordNotes.term: κατευθύναι (kateuthynai) — direct
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to make straight or guide along a direct path. In 1 Thessalonians 3:11 it refers to a literal journey; here, as in several Old Testament prayers, it describes God setting the inner life on a right course.

wordNotes.term: εἰς τὴν ὑπομονὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ (eis tēn hypomonēn tou Christou) — into the patient waiting for Christ
wordNotes.explanation: Hypomonē usually denotes endurance under pressure. The phrase may describe the steadfastness Christ displayed or the patient perseverance of those who await Him. Either way, it calls for a hope that holds firm through difficulty until His appearing.

verses.bibleText: Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With “now we command you,” Paul moves from general encouragement to specific direction. In his first letter he had asked the church to “warn them that are unruly” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). The problem persisted, so he now issues a command and grounds it “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The phrase places the instruction under Christ’s authority; the church was to receive it as the Lord’s will and not as a personal preference of the apostle. Yet Paul still calls his readers “brethren,” and he describes the offender as “every brother.” The disorderly remain family even while they are being corrected.

The instruction is addressed to the whole congregation. Discipline was not left to a few leaders; every member shared responsibility for the health of the body. They were to “withdraw” themselves, a verb that pictures drawing back or keeping one’s distance. In context it means withholding the close, ordinary fellowship that would signal approval, including the shared meals that marked early Christian gatherings. The step was firm but not final. Verse 15 adds that such a person is still to be admonished as a brother, and Paul’s concern throughout is to win him back. Removal from the church is reserved in Scripture for graver and unrepentant cases (1 Corinthians 5:1–5; Matthew 18:17).

The offense is walking “disorderly,” a term used of soldiers who break rank or of anyone who ignores an agreed pattern of life. Verses 10–11 show that the disorder consisted chiefly in refusing to work and in meddling with other people’s affairs. The setting suggests that excitement over Christ’s expected return had led some to treat ordinary labor as pointless, though habits of dependence on wealthy patrons, common in Greek cities, may also have played a part.

The standard is “the tradition which he received of us.” Paul uses tradition here for the apostolic teaching handed on to the converts, whether by word or by letter (2:15). It is not a body of human custom added to Scripture; it is the instruction Christ’s messengers delivered, now preserved in the New Testament. The disorderly could not plead ignorance. They had heard the teaching and had watched it lived out, which is the point of the verses that follow.

wordNotes.term: στέλλεσθαι (stellesthai) — withdraw yourselves
wordNotes.explanation: The middle form of this verb means to keep oneself away from or to hold back. Paul is calling for a deliberate distancing from close fellowship with the disobedient, a measured step meant to awaken them, which verse 14 describes again as having no company with them.

wordNotes.term: ἀτάκτως (ataktōs) — disorderly
wordNotes.explanation: The word describes what is out of order, like a soldier out of rank. In this passage the disorder takes the specific form of refusing to work and defying repeated instruction, so the fault is willful idleness more than mere laziness.

verses.bibleText: For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us: for we behaved not ourselves disorderly among you;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul supports his command with two arguments, and the first is his own example. “For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us.” The word “follow” means to imitate. The Thessalonians did not need new information; they needed only to remember what they had watched for weeks. The apostles had lived among them in an orderly way, keeping step with the gospel they preached.

Imitation was a familiar method of moral instruction in the ancient world, where students learned a way of life by observing a teacher. Paul adopts it without pride, because his own conduct was itself an imitation of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). The Thessalonians had earlier become “followers of us, and of the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 1:6); now they are reminded that this imitation reaches the ordinary business of earning a living.

“We behaved not ourselves disorderly among you” uses the verb form of the word in verse 6. The missionaries had not broken ranks. Whatever excuse the idle members offered, it could not be that their teachers had modeled a life detached from daily responsibility. Every minister of the gospel faces the same test: instruction carries weight only when the life of the teacher confirms it (1 Timothy 4:12; Titus 2:7). A congregation learns at least as much from what it sees as from what it hears.

wordNotes.term: μιμεῖσθαι (mimeisthai) — to follow
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to imitate or copy a pattern of conduct. Paul presents himself and his companions as models because they themselves were following Christ, so imitating them meant learning the Lord’s way in concrete, observable form.

verses.bibleText: Neither did we eat any man's bread for nought; but wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul now describes what orderly conduct looked like. “Neither did we eat any man’s bread for nought.” To eat bread is a biblical way of speaking about receiving one’s daily living (Genesis 3:19; 2 Samuel 9:7). The missionaries accepted no free board. When they sat at someone’s table, they paid for what they received.

Instead they “wrought with labour and travail night and day.” The pair “labour and travail” describes wearying, exhausting toil, and Paul had used the same words in his first letter (1 Thessalonians 2:9). “Night and day” indicates that work filled both ends of the day, likely early hours before dawn and late hours after evening, with preaching and pastoral care fitted in between. Acts identifies Paul’s trade as tentmaking (Acts 18:3), a craft carried on in a workshop where conversations about the gospel could arise naturally.

The purpose was “that we might not be chargeable to any of you.” The verb means to weigh down or burden. Many in the young church were poor, and Paul refused to add to their load. He also knew that traveling teachers who lived off their audiences were common, and he would give no one reason to class the gospel with such enterprises (1 Corinthians 9:12). Even so, he gratefully accepted gifts from the Philippians during his stay (Philippians 4:15–16), which shows that his policy was a matter of wisdom in a particular setting and not a rejection of support. His toil was itself a sermon: love that serves without demanding, after the pattern of the One who came to minister (Mark 10:45).

wordNotes.term: ἐν κόπῳ καὶ μόχθῳ (en kopō kai mochthō) — with labour and travail
wordNotes.explanation: Paul pairs two words for hard work to stress its wearisome, draining character. The same combination appears in his description of apostolic hardships, underscoring that his self-support cost him real effort.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιβαρῆσαι (epibarēsai) — be chargeable
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to place weight on someone, here in the sense of making them bear the cost of one’s food and lodging. Paul worked so that no believer would carry that burden on his account.

verses.bibleText: Not because we have not power, but to make ourselves an ensample unto you to follow us.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul anticipates a misunderstanding. Someone might conclude that preachers have no claim on the support of the church, or that Paul worked because he lacked standing as an apostle. He rules out both: “Not because we have not power.” The word means right or authority. In 1 Corinthians 9 Paul argues at length that those who proclaim the gospel are entitled to live by it, citing the law of Moses, the temple service, and a command of the Lord Himself (1 Corinthians 9:9–14; Luke 10:7). Support for gospel workers is a biblical principle that he never withdrew.

He set that right aside in Thessalonica for a further reason: “to make ourselves an ensample unto you to follow us.” The word “ensample” is typos, a pattern or mold that leaves its impression. Paul’s self-supporting labor was meant to stamp a shape on the church’s life. The argument gains force from the contrast. If an apostle with a legitimate claim to support chose to work long hours, those with no such claim had no excuse for living at others’ expense.

The verse illustrates a principle that runs through Paul’s ministry: freedom is to be used for the good of others. Rights are real, yet love may lay them down when doing so serves the gospel, as Christ laid aside the privileges that were His (1 Corinthians 9:19; Philippians 2:4–7).

wordNotes.term: ἐξουσίαν (exousian) — power
wordNotes.explanation: Here the word means a rightful claim or entitlement, not physical strength. Paul affirms that he possessed the right to be supported by the churches he served, even though he chose not to use it among the Thessalonians.

wordNotes.term: τύπον (typon) — ensample
wordNotes.explanation: A typos is the impression left by a stamp or the pattern from which copies are made. Paul offered his working life as a model for the church to reproduce in its own conduct.

verses.bibleText: For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second argument appeals to teaching. “For even when we were with you, this we commanded you.” The tense suggests repeated instruction; during his short stay Paul returned to this subject more than once. The detail shows how practical his founding ministry was. Alongside the great truths of the gospel and the Second Coming (2:5), he taught new converts how to order their days.

The rule itself is brief and memorable: “if any would not work, neither should he eat.” Similar sentiments appear in Hebrew wisdom and in Greek proverbs, but Paul frames this as a command, and its precision matters. He speaks of one who “would not work,” one who is unwilling. The rule says nothing against the sick, the aged, the disabled, widows without support, or those who seek work and cannot find it. Scripture repeatedly charges God’s people to care for such persons (Deuteronomy 15:7–11; 1 Timothy 5:3–8), and verse 13 urges the church not to tire of doing good. The target is the able-bodied believer who chooses to live on the generosity of others.

The principle rests on God’s design. Before sin entered, Adam was placed in the garden “to dress it and to keep it” (Genesis 2:15); after the fall, bread would come by the sweat of the brow (Genesis 3:19). The fourth commandment joins six days of labor to the Sabbath rest: “Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work” (Exodus 20:9). Work and worship belong to one ordered life. Jesus Himself was known in Nazareth as “the carpenter” (Mark 6:3). Daily work is part of the faithful life God intends, and the hope of Christ’s coming does not cancel it.

Paul’s command also protected the church. Generous believers were being exploited, and the poor who needed help were at risk of being crowded out. By refusing to subsidize willful idleness, the congregation would preserve its charity for those in real need and press the idle toward a better way. The best response to the Advent hope is to be found faithfully at work when the Master returns (Matthew 24:45–46).

wordNotes.term: εἴ τις οὐ θέλει ἐργάζεσθαι (ei tis ou thelei ergazesthai) — if any would not work
wordNotes.explanation: The verb thelō expresses will or desire, so the clause describes refusal, not inability. Paul’s rule is aimed at those who could work and choose not to, leaving the church free to help those who cannot.

wordNotes.term: μηδὲ ἐσθιέτω (mēde esthietō) — neither should he eat
wordNotes.explanation: The third-person imperative makes this a directive for the church’s practice: the community should not supply the daily needs of a member who refuses to work. It reflects the created order in which labor and provision belong together.

verses.bibleText: For we hear that there are some which walk among you disorderly, working not at all, but are busybodies.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For we hear” indicates that a recent report had reached Paul in Corinth, perhaps through the messenger who carried the first letter. The news was specific: “there are some which walk among you disorderly.” Paul is careful with numbers. He says “some,” not the whole church; the majority was obeying (v. 4). Yet the group was large enough and persistent enough to require an extended response.

The description of their conduct contains a wordplay that is hard to carry into English. They were “working not at all, but are busybodies”—in Greek, not working but working around. A rendering such as “not busy, but busybodies” catches some of the sting. Those who had abandoned useful labor had not become still. They filled their unoccupied hours by circling into other people’s concerns, offering opinions, perhaps spreading speculation about the end, and creating friction in the church and among neighbors. Paul warns elsewhere of the same pattern among the idle who wander “from house to house … tattlers also and busybodies” (1 Timothy 5:13).

The link between idleness and meddling is practical wisdom. Time not given to honest work seldom stays empty. Peter places the meddler beside the thief and the evildoer in his list of things no Christian should suffer for (1 Peter 4:15), and Proverbs pictures the one who interferes in another’s quarrel as someone grabbing a dog by the ears (Proverbs 26:17). The person who attends faithfully to his own responsibilities has neither the time nor the appetite to manage everyone else’s.

There was a further cost. Paul had urged the Thessalonians to work with their hands so that they would “walk honestly toward them that are without” (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12). Christians who lived as dependents while stirring up talk gave outsiders reason to scorn the gospel, the very word Paul wanted to run and be glorified (v. 1). Disorder within the church always speaks to the watching world.

wordNotes.term: μηδὲν ἐργαζομένους ἀλλὰ περιεργαζομένους (mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous) — working not at all, but are busybodies
wordNotes.explanation: Paul sets the ordinary verb for working beside a compound form meaning to be busy about things that are not one’s concern. The pun exposes the irony: those who refused productive work were still active, but their energy went into meddling with the affairs of others.

verses.bibleText: Now them that are such we command and exhort by our Lord Jesus Christ, that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here, for the only time in the passage, Paul speaks directly to the offenders, though even now he refers to them indirectly as “them that are such.” He combines two verbs: “we command and exhort.” The first carries apostolic authority; the second is the language of pastoral appeal, the word Paul uses when he chooses to plead instead of order (Philemon 1:8–9). Firmness and tenderness meet in one sentence.

The appeal is made “by our Lord Jesus Christ.” The phrase reminds the idle members that they too belong to Christ. Paul addresses them as people within the fold, called back to a way of life that honors their Lord, and he does not write them off as outsiders.

The content is simple: “that with quietness they work, and eat their own bread.” Quietness here does not mean silence. It describes a settled, undisturbed manner of life, the opposite of the restless agitation of the busybody. Paul had used the related verb in his first letter: “study to be quiet” (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Steady labor would replace meddling, and calm would replace excitement. The phrase “their own bread” answers verse 8, where Paul refused to eat another’s bread without paying. The idle are to provide for themselves as their teachers had done.

The remedy for fevered expectation was a return to ordinary faithfulness. Advent faith shows less in how much one talks about the end than in a life made ready by faithfulness in daily things (Luke 12:42–43). The servant who keeps working while he watches is the one the Master commends. Diligent work, offered to the Lord, becomes an act of worship and a witness to those outside the church (Romans 12:11; Colossians 3:23–24).

wordNotes.term: μετὰ ἡσυχίας (meta hēsychias) — with quietness
wordNotes.explanation: Hēsychia denotes a calm, orderly manner of life free from disturbance. It does not require silence; it contrasts the steady worker with the agitated meddler who unsettles others.

wordNotes.term: τὸν ἑαυτῶν ἄρτον (ton heautōn arton) — their own bread
wordNotes.explanation: The reflexive pronoun is emphatic. The idle are to eat food they have earned, providing their own daily needs instead of depending on the generosity of fellow believers.

verses.bibleText: But ye, brethren, be not weary in well doing.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But ye, brethren” turns from the offenders back to the faithful majority. “Be not weary in well doing” addresses a natural danger. Members who had been supporting others could easily grow disillusioned once they realized that some had taken advantage of them. Disappointment could harden into a refusal to help anyone at all, and Paul guards against that overcorrection.

The verb means to lose heart or give up. Jesus used it when He taught that people “ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luke 18:1), and Paul uses it for persevering in ministry despite discouragement (2 Corinthians 4:1, 16). “Well doing” refers here especially to acts of kindness and practical help. The church was to stop feeding willful idleness without closing its hand to those in actual need: the widow, the sick, the persecuted, the honest worker who has fallen on hard times. Discernment in giving is right; abandoning compassion is not.

The exhortation reaches further as well. Doing good often brings little thanks, and some recipients will abuse it. Galatians 6:9–10 supplies the encouragement that makes perseverance possible: “in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.” Generosity rests on God’s faithfulness more than on the gratitude of those helped. A church that keeps doing good reflects the character of a Father who sends rain on the just and on the unjust (Matthew 5:45).

wordNotes.term: μὴ ἐγκακήσητε (mē enkakēsēte) — be not weary
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to lose motivation or grow discouraged in a worthy course. In the New Testament it consistently appears with a negative, urging believers not to give up in prayer, ministry, or kindness.

wordNotes.term: καλοποιοῦντες (kalopoiountes) — in well doing
wordNotes.explanation: This compound participle means doing what is good or right. In this context it points especially to continued practical help for members in real need, even after some had abused the church’s generosity.

verses.bibleText: And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul expects that some will still refuse. “If any man obey not our word by this epistle” treats disobedience as a real possibility. “Our word by this epistle” points to the instructions just given about work and conduct, and it carries an implicit claim. A letter from the apostle was not mere advice. It bore the authority of the Lord in whose name it was written (v. 6), and the church was to treat it so. Paul’s letters were received from the beginning as the word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13; 2 Peter 3:15–16).

The church’s response has three parts. First, “note that man.” The verb means to mark or take notice of someone. The congregation was to recognize openly who was persisting in disobedience, so that the matter would be neither ignored nor left vague. Second, “have no company with him.” The verb pictures mixing together in close association; Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 5:9–11 for social fellowship, especially at table. Normal intimacy was to be suspended. Third, the purpose: “that he may be ashamed.”

Shame in this sense has a healing goal. The word suggests being turned about, brought to see oneself honestly and to reconsider. In a culture where belonging and honor shaped behavior powerfully, the loss of warm fellowship with the new family in Christ would be keenly felt. For converts who had already lost standing with their pagan neighbors, separation from the church would press hard toward repentance. The aim was conviction leading to change, never humiliation for its own sake.

The verse corrects two opposite errors. One is permissiveness, which treats disobedience as unimportant and so lets it spread. The other is harshness, which disciplines in anger and forgets the goal. Scripture’s pattern is firm accountability carried out by the whole body for the sake of the erring member (Matthew 18:15–17; 2 Corinthians 2:6–8).

wordNotes.term: σημειοῦσθε (sēmeiousthe) — note
wordNotes.explanation: Related to the word for a sign or mark, this verb means to take special notice of someone. Here it calls the congregation to identify the persistently disobedient member clearly, as a first step in loving correction.

wordNotes.term: ἵνα ἐντραπῇ (hina entrapē) — that he may be ashamed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb literally suggests turning in upon oneself and, in the passive, being made ashamed. Paul’s purpose is the kind of shame that produces reflection and repentance, as when he writes to admonish beloved children.

verses.bibleText: Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Discipline can drift into hostility, and Paul closes that door at once: “Yet count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.” The disciplined member is not to be treated as an outsider, an opponent, or someone beyond hope. He remains a brother, and the church’s withdrawal is itself an expression of family concern.

To “admonish” is to put sense into someone, to warn and counsel with correction in view. Paul uses the word for the work of leaders and of believers toward one another (1 Thessalonians 5:12, 14; Colossians 3:16), and he describes his own admonitions as those of a father to his children (1 Corinthians 4:14). Withdrawing close fellowship does not end conversation. The faithful are still to speak to the offender, reason with him, plead with him, and keep the way of return open.

This verse shows that the discipline in view stops short of expulsion. A person cut off altogether would hardly be described as a brother to be admonished. The Thessalonians were to hold together two duties that easily pull apart: refusing to endorse wrong conduct while continuing to love the one who does it.

The model is Christ Himself, who confronted sin with clarity and pursued sinners with patience. Paul expresses the same spirit elsewhere: those who are spiritual should restore an erring brother “in the spirit of meekness,” mindful of their own weakness (Galatians 6:1). Correction that forgets kinship becomes cruelty; kinship that refuses correction becomes neglect. The church is called to carry both truth and grace into its dealings with the straying (James 5:19–20).

wordNotes.term: μὴ ὡς ἐχθρὸν ἡγεῖσθε (mē hōs echthron hēgeisthe) — count him not as an enemy
wordNotes.explanation: The present imperative forbids an ongoing attitude. However firm the discipline, the church must never come to regard the erring member as an adversary to be defeated or discarded.

wordNotes.term: νουθετεῖτε (noutheteite) — admonish
wordNotes.explanation: The verb combines warning with instruction, aiming to correct a person’s thinking and conduct. Paul treats it as a responsibility of loving relationship, exercised by leaders and members alike for the good of the one admonished.

verses.bibleText: Now the Lord of peace himself give you peace always by all means. The Lord be with you all.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The closing opens with a prayer for peace, and its wording is unusual. Elsewhere Paul speaks of “the God of peace” (Romans 15:33; 1 Thessalonians 5:23). Here he writes “the Lord of peace himself,” directing the prayer to Christ in keeping with the emphasis on “the Lord” throughout this letter. Isaiah had named the coming Messiah “The Prince of Peace” (Isaiah 9:6), and Jesus promised His disciples a peace the world cannot give (John 14:27). Paul asks that the One who is Himself the source of peace would give it to His people.

The repetition is emphatic: the Lord of peace is to give peace. The need was plain. The Thessalonians faced persecution from outside (1:4–7), confusion about the day of the Lord (2:1–2), and tension inside the church over the disorderly members (3:6–15). Discipline especially could strain relationships, and Paul knew that firm correction needed to be surrounded by grace. Peace in Scripture is more than the absence of conflict. It is the wholeness and well-being that flow from reconciliation with God (Romans 5:1), expressed in harmony among His people (Ephesians 2:14–17).

“Always by all means” widens the prayer to cover every season and circumstance, persecution or calm, clarity or perplexity. The peace Christ gives does not wait for favorable conditions; it guards the heart and mind in the middle of them (Philippians 4:7).

“The Lord be with you all” echoes a greeting rooted in Israel’s history. Boaz greeted his reapers with it (Ruth 2:4), and the angel used similar words to address Gideon (Judges 6:12). In those settings “the Lord” is the God of Israel; Paul applies the greeting to Jesus, whose presence is the church’s security. The added “all” is pointed. It includes the anxious and the steadfast, the faithful majority and the disorderly few under correction. No member is left outside the prayer that Christ would be near. Those under discipline needed His presence as much as anyone, and the Lord who corrects is the same Lord who stays close.

wordNotes.term: ὁ κύριος τῆς εἰρήνης (ho kyrios tēs eirēnēs) — the Lord of peace
wordNotes.explanation: Paul’s usual phrase is “the God of peace.” Substituting “Lord” directs the prayer to Christ, presenting Him as both the possessor and the giver of peace, the One in whom believers are reconciled to God and to one another.

wordNotes.term: διὰ παντὸς ἐν παντὶ τρόπῳ (dia pantos en panti tropō) — always by all means
wordNotes.explanation: The two phrases extend the prayer across all times and all circumstances. A few manuscripts read “in every place,” but “in every way” is better supported and suits the many kinds of trouble the letter addresses.

verses.bibleText: The salutation of Paul with mine own hand, which is the token in every epistle: so I write.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
At this point Paul takes the pen from his scribe. Ancient letters were commonly dictated to a secretary, and the sender often added a closing line in his own handwriting. Paul mentions doing so in several letters (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18), and one of his scribes even adds a personal greeting (Romans 16:22). Here, however, he explains the practice: “which is the token in every epistle: so I write.”

The explanation suits this letter’s situation. The Thessalonians had been disturbed by a message “as from us” claiming that the day of Christ was already present (2:2). Whether it came through a forged letter or a supposed prophetic word attributed to Paul, the danger of counterfeit authority was real. By drawing attention to his handwriting, Paul gave the church a way to recognize what came from him and to reject what did not. The word “token” means a sign or mark of identification. “In every epistle” indicates that this was his regular custom, even where he did not mention it.

The signature also made Paul’s presence felt. Though absent, he stands behind every word of the letter, including the hard instructions about discipline. No one could dismiss those commands as the opinion of someone else writing in his name.

The verse is a reminder that God’s people need not be at the mercy of every claim to speak for Him. The church is to test messages by the authentic apostolic word (Galatians 1:8–9; 1 John 4:1). Scripture, faithfully preserved, remains the standard by which every teaching about Christ and His coming must be measured (Isaiah 8:20).

wordNotes.term: ὁ ἀσπασμὸς τῇ ἐμῇ χειρὶ Παύλου (ho aspasmos tē emē cheiri Paulou) — the salutation of Paul with mine own hand
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase marks the shift from the scribe’s writing to Paul’s own. Because his letters were read aloud to gathered congregations, he names the change so that hearers who could not see the page would know that the apostle himself had signed it.

wordNotes.term: σημεῖον (sēmeion) — token
wordNotes.explanation: A sēmeion is a sign by which something is recognized. The relative pronoun that introduces the clause refers to the fact of Paul’s handwriting, which served as a mark of genuineness against messages falsely claiming his authority.

verses.bibleText: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter ends where every letter of Paul ends, with grace. “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.” It opened with “Grace unto you, and peace” (1:2); peace has now been prayed for in verse 16 and grace closes the letter, so the two words frame the whole.

The wording nearly matches the end of the first letter (1 Thessalonians 5:28), with one addition: “all.” As in verse 16, the word reaches every member. The anxious who feared they had missed the day of the Lord, the persecuted who longed for rest, the faithful who had grown weary of supporting others, and the idle who needed correction are all included. The grace that saves sinners is the same grace that trains them in obedience and restores them when they stray (Titus 2:11–13).

The closing “Amen” is absent from some early manuscripts and may have been added in later copying. The note found at the end of some editions, stating that the letter was written from Athens, is also a later addition; Acts and the letters themselves point to Corinth. Neither detail affects the message. The final word belongs to the grace of Christ, which carries His people from their first believing until His appearing.

wordNotes.term: ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ (hē charis tou kyriou hēmōn Iēsou Christou) — the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ
wordNotes.explanation: Grace is God’s unearned favor and enabling power, given through Christ. Paul’s final wish asks that this favor remain with the church, supplying pardon, strength, and perseverance until the Lord returns.

wordNotes.term: μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν (meta pantōn hymōn) — with you all
wordNotes.explanation: The word “all” is added to Paul’s usual closing here. It embraces every member of the congregation, including those under discipline, as recipients of Christ’s grace.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How should hope in Christ’s return shape the way a believer prays, works, and treats a fellow member who has gone astray?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The faithful Lord who will return calls His waiting people to pray for the gospel’s progress, to work responsibly, and to correct one another in love, while He supplies peace and grace to all.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul ask first for the progress of the word before asking for his own safety?
How does the contrast between human unbelief and the Lord’s faithfulness steady a believer under pressure?
What does Paul’s decision to support himself by manual labor teach about leadership and example?
How do verses 14 and 15 keep church discipline from becoming either careless or harsh?
Why does Paul twice include “you all” in his final blessings?
commonMisunderstandings: Verse 10 does not withhold help from those unable to work because of illness, age, disability, or lack of opportunity; it addresses those unwilling to work.
Withdrawing from a disorderly member does not mean treating him as an enemy or expelling him from the family of faith; the aim is repentance and restoration.
Expecting Christ’s return gives no warrant for abandoning ordinary duties; faithful waiting includes faithful work.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the chapter’s balance: firm standards with tender relationships, Advent hope with daily labor, and apostolic command with dependence on the Lord who enables obedience.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Ask the faithful Lord to direct your heart into God’s love and Christ’s steadfastness, then take up today’s work and today’s relationships as one who is waiting for Him.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The faithful Lord Jesus keeps those who trust Him, guards them from the evil one, and calls them to a life of steady hope and useful work until His return.
flow: Many reject the gospel, and the conflict between Christ and Satan is real.
Christ remains faithful when people are not, and He promises to establish and guard those who come to Him.
His love becomes the settled home of the heart, and His steadfastness becomes the believer’s pattern.
Saved by grace, believers serve Him in ordinary work, honest dealing, and patient hope.
Those who wait for His appearing may begin that life now by trusting Him.
simpleIllustrations: A runner carrying an urgent message needs an open road; prayer helps clear the road for the gospel.
A sentry at a city gate protects those inside who could not defend themselves; Christ stands guard over the people who trust Him.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you trust the faithful Lord to establish you, keep you, and direct your heart into His love as you wait for His coming?
cautions: Do not use verse 10 to shame the poor, the sick, or the unemployed who are willing to work.
Do not present Christ’s protection as a promise of freedom from every hardship.
Do not set the Advent hope against diligent, responsible living.

reflectionQuestions: Whom am I praying for so that the word of the Lord may run freely through their witness?
Where do I need to rest on the Lord’s faithfulness instead of on how people respond to me?
Does my hope in Christ’s return make me more faithful in ordinary work, or more restless?
When someone in my church drifts, do I avoid them, attack them, or admonish them as family?
What would it look like for the Lord of peace to give me peace “by all means” this week?
